name: Mongol Conquest of Song Dynasty
description: Mongol conquest under Kublai Khan. Final Chinese dynasty fell to foreign rulers, establishing Yuan Dynasty.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Mongol conquest of the Song Dynasty
casualtyRange.notes: 1205-1279. Song conquest component of broader Mongol expansion. Siege and conquest casualties.

hook: Kublai Khan conquered the Song Dynasty (1276-1279), completing Mongol conquest of China and establishing the Yuan Dynasty.
narrative: After his grandfather Genghis Khan's invasions of northern China, Kublai Khan systematically conquered the southern Song Dynasty (1276-1279). Naval battles and siege warfare saw Chinese resistance gradually overwhelmed. Song dynasty fell; Kublai established Yuan Dynasty (1279-1368) with Chinese administration. The conquest was relatively bloodless compared to earlier Mongol invasions. Perhaps 1+ million died in conquest and subsequent famines. The Yuan Dynasty was eventually overthrown by Han Chinese Ming Dynasty (1368), restoring Han rule.
significance: Kublai Khan's conquest unified all China under Mongol rule. The Yuan Dynasty demonstrated that foreign conquerors could adopt Chinese administrative traditions and legitimacy. Kublai's rule was relatively stable; trade flourished. However, the Yuan Dynasty's foreigner status created resentment that contributed to its eventual overthrow. Kublai remains controversial: celebrated as great conqueror by Mongols; seen as invader by Chinese. The conquest shows how military conquest could be legitimized through cultural adoption.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Mongol Conquest of Song Dynasty
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Mongol Conquest of China
description: The Mongols' conquest of the Jin Dynasty and later the Song Dynasty, establishing Yuan Dynasty rule over China.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Mongol conquest of China; Clodfelter
casualtyRange.notes: China-specific Mongol expansion. Population fell ~50% during Jin-Yuan transition (1205-1279).

hook: Genghis Khan's successors conquered all of China (1205-1279), establishing Mongol Yuan Dynasty and demonstrating conquest's military supremacy.
narrative: Genghis Khan invaded the Jin Dynasty (northern China) in 1205. His successors continued conquest through 1279, when Kublai Khan completed the conquest of the Song Dynasty. China's population fell from 123 million (1200) to perhaps 60-80 million by 1300, due to warfare, massacre, and famine. Entire cities were razed; agricultural regions abandoned. Mongols adopted Chinese administrative practices but maintained military supremacy. Yuan Dynasty (1279-1368) ruled until Han Chinese Ming dynasty restored Han rule.
significance: Mongol conquest of China showed that military superiority could overcome civilizational advantage. The conquest killed tens of millions. Kublai Khan's establishment of Yuan Dynasty demonstrated foreign conquerors' need to adopt indigenous legitimacy. The Yuan Dynasty's eventual overthrow showed that foreign rule required cultural assimilation or would face persistent resistance. Modern China views the Mongol invasion as a cautionary tale of vulnerability. The conquest influenced Chinese nationalism and historical consciousness about defense against 'barbarian' invasion.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Mongol Conquests
description: Genghis Khan's establishment of the Mongol Empire and the extensive conquests that created the largest land empire ever.

casualtyRange.notes: Aggregate deaths across Central Asia, Persia, China, Eastern Europe 1206-1368. High estimates exceed 100M including indirect effects.

hook: Genghis Khan unified steppe tribes to create history's largest land empire through unmatched cavalry tactics.
narrative: In 1206, Temüjin (later Genghis Khan) united feuding Mongol clans and organized them into a military machine based on meritocracy and discipline. The Mongols employed composite bows, lightning cavalry maneuvers, and psychological warfare to overwhelm settled civilizations. By 1368, the Mongol Empire stretched from the Pacific to Eastern Europe. Key turning points included the 1202 victories over Tartars and Kereit, the 1211 invasion of the Jin Dynasty (breaking the wall myth), and the rapid succession of campaigns across Central Asia, the Middle East, and China. The Mongols established the Pax Mongolica, enabling trade on the Silk Road and spreading military, administrative, and technological knowledge across Eurasia.
significance: Mongol rule connected east and west like never before, facilitating unprecedented technology transfer (from gunpowder to papermaking). The Mongol invasions decimated numerous civilizations but paradoxically created the conditions for cultural exchange, scientific advancement, and the global medieval economy. Their administrative practices influenced Ottoman and Russian imperial systems.

name: Mongol Invasion of the Middle East
description: The Mongol conquests under Genghis Khan and his successors that devastated the Islamic world.
hook: Hulagu Khan's Mongol armies shattered the Islamic Golden Age, sacking Baghdad and ending the Abbasid Caliphate.
narrative: Under Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu, Mongol armies invaded the Islamic heartland in 1219, conquering Khorasan and Persia. The Mongols crushed major cities—Nishapur, Balkh, Gur (Gurgan)—with devastating cavalry assaults. The climactic moment came in 1258 when Hulagu's forces besieged Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, and after a brief defense, sacked it. The caliph al-Musta'sim was killed, the city's libraries burned, and hundreds of thousands perished. The Mongol invasion scattered Islamic centers of learning and shattered the political unity of the Islamic world. The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt halted Mongol expansion westward at the Battle of Ayn Jalut (1260).
significance: The fall of Baghdad symbolized the end of the Islamic Golden Age and the fragmentation of the Islamic world into competing regional powers. The destruction of libraries and intellectual centers devastated Islamic scholarship temporarily. However, the Mongol conquest also facilitated cultural and technological exchange and eventually led to the rise of the Ottoman Empire as Islam's new superpower.

name: Mayapan-Chichén Itzá War
description: Conflict between the two dominant Yucatán Maya centers. Mayapan's victory established it as the dominant Postclassic Maya power, lasting until its fall in 1441.
hook: Post-Classic Maya hegemonic conflict established Mayapan's dominance over Yucatan peninsula.
narrative: Mayapan, a city-state in western Yucatan, challenged Chichen Itza's hegemony in the 12th century. Military conflict resulted in Chichen Itza's decline and Mayapan's rise as the peninsula's dominant power. The war involved alliances with neighboring states and mercenary forces. Mayapan organized a confederated governance system for the peninsula.
significance: Mayapan victory established a new hegemonic center for Yucatan. The confederate system temporarily unified Post-Classic Maya territories.

name: Sundiata's Mandinka Conquests
description: Sundiata Keita's military campaigns that founded the Mali Empire and defeated the Sosso Kingdom.
hook: Sundiata founded the Mali Empire (1230s) through military conquest, creating West Africa's first great empire and spreading Islam.
narrative: Sundiata Keita, a Mandinka warlord, united Mandinka clans and conquered neighboring territories (1230s-1260s). He defeated the Sosso Empire and established Mali as a regional superpower. Sundiata's empire controlled major trade routes (salt, gold, ivory). Islam spread as Sundiata adopted it as state religion. The Mali Empire flourished for two centuries (until replaced by Songhai empire, 1470s). Sundiata's conquests created one of the medieval world's largest empires. Thousands died in conquest; exact figures are unknown.
significance: Sundiata's conquests created Mali—West Africa's first great documented empire. The empire's gold wealth made it known across Mediterranean and Islamic world. Mali's example influenced subsequent African state-building. Sundiata's legend (preserved in griots' oral tradition) became the model for African heroic epics. Mali's Islamic adoption shaped West African religious identity. Modern Mali's nationalism invokes Sundiata as founder-hero. The empire's gold gave West Africa economic power that made it attractive for European trade (later slave trade).

narrative: Mali Empire expanded across West Africa through systematic military campaigns. Sundiata's victories established Mali dominance over the former Ghana Empire territories. Subsequent emperors continued expansion, consolidating control over gold and salt trade routes. Mali's military organization included cavalry units and administrative integration.
significance: Mali expansion established West African political unity and trade dominance. The empire created administrative templates for successor states.

narrative: Bamako, strategically located on the Niger River, fell to Mali military campaigns. The conquest secured Mali control of critical river trade routes. Bamako's integration into Mali strengthened Mali's commercial dominance.
significance: Bamako's conquest completed Mali's Niger valley control and secured trade route dominance.

name: Yuan Conquest of Southern China
description: Final phase of Mongol conquest of southern Song territory and capitals.
hook: Mongol forces systematically conquered the Southern Song Dynasty, ending a century of divided Chinese rule.
narrative: The Mongol Yuan Dynasty had conquered northern China by 1234; southern China remained under the Song Dynasty until the 1270s. Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, launched a systematic invasion of Song territories. Key battles included the naval Battle of Yamen (1279), where Song forces were defeated and the Song emperor drowned, ending the dynasty. Mongol cavalry and siege warfare gradually overwhelmed Song resistance. Cities like Xiangyang held out but eventually fell to superior numbers and logistics. By 1279, all of China was under Mongol rule. The conquest involved tens of thousands of soldiers and lasted nearly a decade.
significance: The Mongol conquest unified China under foreign rule for the first time. The Yuan Dynasty adopted Chinese administrative practices but maintained Mongol military supremacy and ethnic privileges. The conquest demonstrated the superiority of nomadic cavalry tactics over settled populations. However, the Yuan's authoritarian policies and Mongol privilege sparked resentment, leading to the Ming Dynasty's restoration in 1368.

narrative: The Iroquois Confederacy expanded against neighboring Algonquian-speaking peoples throughout the pre-Columbian and early colonial periods. Conflicts intensified dramatically in the 17th century with the Beaver Wars. Iroquois warfare combined strategic military organization with adoption-based population maintenance. These conflicts reshaped northeastern North American indigenous demography.
significance: Iroquois military dominance established the Confederacy's regional hegemony and influenced colonial North American politics. The conflicts facilitated French-English colonial competition.

narrative: Somali sultanates including Adal, Ajuran, and others competed for dominance over East African territories. Wars involved territorial conquest, trade route control, and religious authority. Somali sultanates expanded southward against other indigenous peoples.
significance: Somali sultanate conflicts established Somali predominance in the Horn of Africa. The sultanates' militarization presaged later confrontations with colonial powers.

name: Hundred Years' War
description: The prolonged conflict between England and France over succession to the French throne, lasting over a century.

casualtyRange.notes: France-England 1337-1453. Military deaths ~150k; civilians 1.5-4M from warfare, plague, famine.

hook: England and France fought intermittently for 116 years over the English throne, reshaping European national identity.
narrative: English kings claimed France's crown after the 1328 death of Charles IV, sparking the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453). Early English victories exploited longbow technology at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415). Joan of Arc's 1429-1431 campaigns inspired French resistance. The war devastated France's countryside; Norman holdings in France shifted repeatedly. Gunpowder artillery increasingly outmatched castles. By 1453, English forces withdrew from France except Calais (lost 1558). Thousands died in battles and from war-induced famines.
significance: The war forged French and English national identities distinct from feudal overlordship. Artillery's rise made medieval fortifications obsolete, spurring the transition to early modern warfare. Joan of Arc became an enduring symbol of French nationalism. The war accelerated state centralization in both kingdoms. England's continental ambitions, thwarted after 1453, redirected English naval power toward colonial expansion.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Aztec Expansion
description: The Aztecs' military campaigns that established their empire through conquest of surrounding city-states.
hook: Mexica/Aztec imperial expansion conquered dozens of Mesoamerican city-states through military campaigns.
narrative: The Aztec Empire, centered at Tenochtitlan, expanded through military conquest under successive emperors. Montezuma I (1440-1468) launched systematic campaigns against neighboring kingdoms, establishing tributary relationships. Subsequent emperors expanded the empire to encompass over 600 subject city-states. Aztec strategy combined direct military conquest with tributary diplomacy. The empire extracted tribute in goods, labor, and captives for sacrifice.
significance: Aztec imperial expansion created the largest Mesoamerican political unit before Spanish conquest. The tributary system's oppressive burden motivated indigenous allies to support Cortés.

name: Early Aztec Expansion
description: Early Aztec campaigns establishing the Mexica as a major power.

name: Battle of Crécy
description: The English victory using longbows against French knights, marking the decline of medieval cavalry.

name: Mutapa-Zimbabwe Wars
description: Conflicts and territorial disputes between Great Zimbabwe and the rising Mutapa Empire.
hook: Mutapa Empire and Zimbabwe Kingdom competed for dominance in southern African interior.
narrative: The Mutapa Empire, centered in modern Zimbabwe and Mozambique, contested regional dominance against the Zimbabwe Kingdom. Military campaigns involved territorial disputes and trade route control. The conflicts shaped southern African political organization.
significance: Mutapa-Zimbabwe conflicts established political boundaries for southern African states. The conflicts presaged later European colonization.

name: Red Turban Rebellion
description: Massive peasant uprising against Yuan Mongol rule. Led to establishment of Ming Dynasty by Zhu Yuanzhang.
hook: A millenarian religious uprising shattered Yuan Dynasty rule and ushered in the Ming Dynasty's establishment.
narrative: The Red Turban Rebellion (1351-1368) was a major peasant uprising against the Mongol Yuan Dynasty. The rebellion was inspired by White Lotus millenarian Buddhism and Daoism. Red Turban forces spread across southern and central China, attacking Yuan garrisons. Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant-soldier, rose through the Red Turban ranks to command the most powerful faction. While other Red Turban leaders fragmented into rival factions, Zhu Yuanzhang consolidated power and defeated competing warlords. By 1368, Zhu declared the establishment of the Ming Dynasty and drove the Yuan north. The rebellion combined religious ideology with peasant grievances and military innovation.
significance: The Red Turban Rebellion demonstrated the power of religious ideology in mobilizing peasant revolts. The rebellion's success established the Ming Dynasty, which ruled China for 276 years and represented a Han Chinese restoration after Mongol rule. The rebellion's use of religious symbols (red turbans) influenced subsequent uprisings. The Ming's founding through the rebellion shaped the dynasty's initial policies toward peasants and the military.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Lao-Siamese Wars
description: Long rivalry between Lao and Siamese kingdoms.
hook: Lao kingdoms and Siamese (Thai) powers contested for mainland Southeast Asian dominance.
narrative: Lao kingdoms, particularly Lan Xang, conducted conflicts with Thai Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. Wars involved territorial disputes and tributary relationships. The conflicts established boundaries between Thai and Lao regions.
significance: Lao-Siamese conflicts defined modern Thailand-Laos boundaries. The wars prevented either side from establishing complete hegemony.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Balkans
description: Ottoman expansion brought the entire Balkan peninsula under Ottoman control over two centuries, establishing Ottoman dominance in Southeastern Europe. This conquest lasted for nearly 400 years.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Ottoman conquest of the Balkans
casualtyRange.notes: 1354-1521. Aggregate casualties from Ottoman expansion into Balkans. High estimates include indirect effects.

hook: Ottoman Empire's military expansion conquered the Balkans and established Ottoman European dominance.
narrative: Ottoman forces, particularly under Murad I and Mehmed II, systematically conquered Balkan territories. Major victories at Maritza (1365) and Kosovo (1389) broke Balkan resistance. By the 15th century, Ottoman dominance over the Balkans was complete. The conquest displaced Christian populations and Islamicized the region.
significance: Ottoman Balkan conquest established Ottoman European power and presaged the empire's eastward expansion. The conquest created the Ottoman-Christian border that persisted for centuries.

name: Battle of Poitiers
description: Another English victory capturing the French king John II, further humiliating France.
hook: 1356 English victory in the Hundred Years' War demonstrated longbow superiority and English dominance.
narrative: English forces under Edward, the Black Prince, defeated French forces at Poitiers in 1356. The victory demonstrated English military tactics and longbow effectiveness. King John II of France was captured. The victory dramatically shifted Hundred Years' War balance toward England.
significance: Poitiers' victory solidified English military dominance and enabled English territorial expansion in France. The battle became iconic for English military superiority.

name: Ava Empire Conflicts
description: Ava kingdom's conflicts with neighboring Shan states.
hook: Ava Empire of Burma conducted military campaigns establishing regional Burmese dominance.
narrative: The Ava Empire, centered in central Burma, conducted military campaigns against rival Burmese kingdoms and neighboring powers. Ava military organization included cavalry and fortifications. The empire expanded territorial control through conquest.
significance: Ava establishment of Burmese regional dominance influenced Southeast Asian politics. The empire's administrative systems influenced successor Burmese dynasties.

name: Bahmani-Vijayanagara Wars
description: Centuries-long conflict between Islamic Bahmani and Hindu Vijayanagara.
hook: Hindu Vijayanagara Empire and Muslim Bahmani Sultanate contested for control of southern Indian territories.
narrative: The Bahmani Sultanate, an Islamic power in southern India, conducted sustained warfare against the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire. The conflicts involved siege warfare, cavalry battles, and capture of strategic cities. The wars created a frontier dynamic characterized by periodic major conflicts.
significance: Bahmani-Vijayanagara conflicts established the pattern of Hindu-Muslim political competition in South India. The conflicts prevented either power from establishing unchallenged dominance.

name: Serbian-Ottoman Wars
description: The conflicts between the Serbian kingdom and the Ottoman Empire that resulted in Ottoman conquest.
hook: Serbian kingdoms resisted Ottoman expansion in the Balkans through military campaigns.
narrative: Serbian forces under leaders like Lazar Hrebeljanović conducted resistance against Ottoman conquest. Major battles at Kosovo (1389) and Maritza (1365) demonstrated Serbian military capacity. However, Ottoman military superiority and numerical advantages eventually overwhelmed Serbian resistance.
significance: Serbian resistance to Ottoman conquest presaged centuries of Christian-Muslim conflict in the Balkans. Serbian military heroism became foundational to Serbian national identity.

name: Vijayanagara-Bahmani Wars
description: The prolonged conflict between the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire and the Islamic Bahmani Sultanate for control of the Deccan.
hook: Hindu Vijayanagara Empire and Muslim Bahmani Sultanate fought multiple wars for southern Indian dominance.
narrative: The Vijayanagara Empire, a major Hindu power, conducted sustained warfare against the Bahmani Sultanate. Battles involved large cavalry forces, elephants, and siege warfare. The wars lasted centuries with alternating periods of dominance and peace.
significance: Vijayanagara-Bahmani conflicts shaped South Indian political geography and religious-political organization. The wars demonstrated Hindu military capability against Islamic powers.

name: Ming Dynasty Conflicts
description: The conflicts during early Ming Dynasty consolidation of power against Mongol remnants and internal threats.
hook: Ming Dynasty maintained internal order through military campaigns against rebels and regional powers.
narrative: The Ming Dynasty faced internal rebellions and provincial conflicts. Military campaigns suppressed revolts and maintained imperial authority. The dynasty's military organization evolved to manage frontier defense and internal stability.
significance: Ming military strength maintained dynastic stability. The dynasty's military innovations influenced subsequent Chinese dynasties.

name: Timurid Invasions
description: Timur's invasion campaigns that devastated Central Asia, the Middle East, and parts of India.
hook: Timur the Conqueror carved a vast empire through devastation and strategic genius, reshaping Central Asia and the Middle East.
narrative: Timur (Tamerlane), a Mongol-descended warlord from Samarkand, built an empire through ruthless military campaigns (1369-1405). He conquered the Ottoman Empire, defeated the Golden Horde, and invaded India and the Middle East. Timur's armies employed psychological terror—wholesale destruction of cities that resisted, pyramids of skulls—to discourage further opposition. Key victories included defeating the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara (1402) and raiding Delhi (1398). Timur's sons inherited fragments of his empire; his grandson Ulugh Beg became a patron of astronomy and culture in Samarkand.
significance: Timur's conquests revitalized the Silk Road and made Samarkand a cosmopolitan center of learning and art. Although destructive, his reign temporarily unified Central Asia and influenced the rise of the Timurid dynasty (15th century) as patrons of Persian culture. Timur's legacy influenced Ottoman political strategy and demonstrated the vulnerability of empires to nomadic invasions.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

casualtyRange.source: Islamic and Central Asian records; Clodfelter

name: Zhu Yuanzhang's Northern Expedition
description: Ming founder's campaigns eliminating Yuan remnants and establishing Ming rule.
hook: A peasant-soldier's military campaign expelled the Mongol Yuan Dynasty and established Han Chinese rule.
narrative: Zhu Yuanzhang (1328-1398), born a peasant, rose through the ranks of the Red Turban Rebellion to become the most powerful warlord in southern China. After consolidating control over southern territories through military campaigns (1356-1368), Zhu launched the Northern Expedition to capture the Yuan Dynasty's heartland. His armies, numbering over 250,000, advanced northward through coordinated campaigns. Key victories included the capture of major cities like Yangzhou, Nanjing, and eventually Beijing (1368). The Yuan emperor and court fled to Mongolia. By 1368, Zhu declared himself emperor and established the Ming Dynasty. The Northern Expedition resulted in the complete expulsion of the Mongol Yuan Dynasty from China proper.
significance: Zhu Yuanzhang's Northern Expedition restored Han Chinese rule over China and established the Ming Dynasty, which ruled China for 276 years. The expedition's success demonstrated the power of peasant military mobilization and meritocratic leadership. The Ming Dynasty's founding through military conquest shaped its authoritarian and military-focused governance. The expedition established Ming control over China and its restoration of Han rule influenced subsequent Chinese national identity. The Ming's subsequent policies and cultural achievements made it one of China's most celebrated dynasties.

name: Timurid Conquests
description: Timur's conquests created brief empire across Central Asia and into Middle East and India.
hook: Timur's empire stretched from Anatolia to India, establishing a legacy of military innovation and cultural achievement.
narrative: Timur (1336-1405) was a military genius who unified fragmented Turco-Mongol tribes through conquest. His campaigns from 1370-1405 conquered Mesopotamia, the Levant, Anatolia (defeating Bayezid I in 1402), Persia, and India. Timur's strategy combined rapid cavalry deployment with siege engineering; his forces sacked Damascus, Baghdad, and Delhi. The conquest of the Ottoman Sultan demonstrated Timur's supremacy even over established empires. His court at Samarkand gathered architects, poets, and scholars. After his death in 1405, his sons divided the empire; the Timurid dynasty (especially under Ulugh Beg and later patrons) became celebrated for astronomy, mathematics, and Persian art.
significance: Timurid rule established Samarkand as a center of Islamic learning and art (the Timurid Renaissance). The conquest temporarily unified Central Asia and influenced Ottoman administrative practices. Timur's legacy shaped the political development of the Middle East and Central Asia, and his military innovations influenced subsequent empires.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Toktamish-Ming Conflicts
description: Ming conflicts with western Mongol leaders.
hook: Toktamish Khan of the Golden Horde and Ming Dynasty competed for dominance across Central Asia and Mongolia.
narrative: Toktamish, a powerful Mongol khan, conducted campaigns in Central Asia and threatened Ming Dynasty interests. The conflicts involved steppe cavalry warfare and territorial disputes. Ming military pressure limited Toktamish expansion.
significance: Toktamish-Ming conflicts shaped Central Asian and East Asian geopolitics. The conflicts demonstrated Ming military reach into Central Asia.

name: War of Chioggia
description: The final conflict between Venice and Genoa that established Venice's dominance in the Mediterranean.
hook: Late 14th-century naval conflict between Venice and Genoa for control of Mediterranean trade.
narrative: The War of Chioggia (1379-1380) represented the final major conflict between Venice and Genoa, two Mediterranean maritime powers. Naval battles, amphibious operations, and siege warfare characterized the conflict. Venice ultimately prevailed, establishing Venetian Mediterranean dominance.
significance: Chioggia's outcome definitively established Venetian Mediterranean dominance. The victory ended Genoa's competitive maritime challenge to Venice.

name: Oura Wars
description: Japanese raids and conflicts involving Korean forces in Kyushu.
hook: Conflicts in Oura region of West Africa involved regional power competition.
narrative: Oura region conflicts involved local kingdoms and ethnic groups competing for territorial control. Wars shaped regional political organization and influenced West African trade networks.
significance: Oura conflicts established regional political boundaries. The wars influenced West African political geography.

name: Burmese-Siamese Wars (14th-15th centuries)
description: First period of Burmese-Siamese conflicts over regional dominance in mainland Southeast Asia.
hook: Medieval Burma and Siam (Thailand) conducted recurring military conflicts for mainland Southeast Asian dominance.
narrative: Pagan and Ava (Burmese powers) and Sukhothai and Ayutthaya (Thai powers) conducted recurring conflicts. Wars involved siege warfare, naval operations, and diplomatic intrigue. The conflicts established boundaries between Burmese and Thai spheres.
significance: Burmese-Siamese conflicts prevented either power from establishing complete mainland dominance. The wars established geopolitical patterns lasting centuries.

name: Battle of Kosovo
description: The famous battle where Serbian Prince Lazar confronted Ottoman Sultan Murad I, resulting in Serbian defeat and Ottoman expansion.
hook: 1389 battle between Serbian and Ottoman forces marked a pivotal moment in Balkan conquest.
narrative: The Battle of Kosovo (1389) between Serbian forces under Lazar Hrebeljanović and Ottoman forces under Murad I is remembered as a defining moment in Serbian-Ottoman conflict. Though tactically inconclusive, the battle presaged Ottoman ultimate victory. Serbian military heroism became legendary.
significance: Kosovo became symbolic of Serbian resistance and loss. The battle's commemoration influenced Serbian national identity for centuries.

name: Kingdom of Kongo Expansion
description: Military campaigns of the Kingdom of Kongo establishing dominance in Central Africa.
hook: Kongo Kingdom expanded territorial control through military conquest in Central Africa.
narrative: The Kongo Kingdom, a major Central African power, expanded through military campaigns against neighboring groups. Kongo military organization and trade networks facilitated territorial expansion. The kingdom integrated conquered populations through administrative incorporation.
significance: Kongo expansion established Central African political dominance. The kingdom's administrative systems influenced later colonial governance.

name: Kalmar Union Wars
description: Nordic union conflicts establishing Swedish separation.
hook: The Kalmar Union established Nordic political unity through military conflicts and dynastic diplomacy.
narrative: Margaret I of Denmark united Scandinavia through military campaigns and dynastic arrangements. Conflicts involved suppression of internal revolts and defense against external threats. The Kalmar Union created a major Nordic power.
significance: Kalmar Union established Nordic political organization persisting into the modern era. The union influenced Baltic regional geopolitics.

name: Timur's Invasion of Delhi
description: Timur's invasion and sack of Delhi that devastated the city and the Indian subcontinent.
hook: Timur's 1398 invasion devastated Delhi and demonstrated steppe warrior dominance over settled empires.
narrative: Timur's Central Asian forces invaded northern India in 1398, targeting the Delhi Sultanate. Timur's army sacked Delhi, killed vast populations, and captured treasures. The invasion devastated northern Indian civilization. Timur's forces withdrew with plunder.
significance: Delhi's sack demonstrated Indian vulnerability to steppe invasion. The invasion presaged subsequent Central Asian incursions into India.

name: Timurid Invasion of India
description: Timur's devastating raid on Delhi, sacking the city and massacring inhabitants.
hook: Timurid forces invaded northern India, bringing Central Asian military technology and organization.
narrative: Timurid invasions of India, particularly Timur's 1398 campaign, devastated the Delhi Sultanate and northern Indian civilization. The invasions demonstrated steppe cavalry superiority and established Timurid power in the region. However, Timurid occupation did not persist.
significance: Timurid invasions exposed Indian vulnerabilities to Central Asian military superiority. The invasions influenced Indian military and political development.

name: Apache-Pueblo Conflicts
description: Long-term conflicts between Apache raiders and settled Pueblo peoples. Apache migration into Southwest region disrupted established Pueblo trade networks.
hook: Pre-colonial Apache raiding and trade conflicts with settled Pueblo peoples shaped Southwestern North American frontier dynamics.
narrative: Apache and Pueblo interactions involved both trade and raiding relationships. Apache, nomadic pastoralists, conducted raids against Pueblo settlements to acquire goods, captives, and prestige. Pueblo defenses included fortified settlements and coordinated militia responses. The balance of power shifted periodically as Apache groups gained access to horses and firearms. Spanish colonization disrupted these established dynamics.
significance: Apache-Pueblo conflicts presaged the multi-sided conflicts characterizing Spanish colonial North America. The interactions demonstrated indigenous frontier dynamics preceding European arrival.

name: Benin Kingdom Wars
description: Military campaigns and conquests of the Benin Kingdom establishing West African dominance.
hook: Benin Kingdom of West Africa conducted military campaigns establishing regional West African dominance.
narrative: The Benin Kingdom, located in modern Nigeria, conducted military campaigns against neighboring peoples. Benin warriors were famous for their discipline and military organization. The kingdom expanded territorial control and wealth through military success.
significance: Benin military dominance established the kingdom as a major West African power. Benin's military organization influenced West African warfare.

name: Kanem-Bornu-Tuareg Conflicts
description: Conflicts between Kanem-Bornu and Tuareg raiders across the Saharan frontier.
hook: The Kanem-Bornu Empire and Tuareg nomads competed for control of Saharan and Sahelian territories.
narrative: The Kanem-Bornu, a major Saharan power, conducted conflicts with Tuareg nomads for territorial control and trade route dominance. Wars involved cavalry combat and siege warfare. The conflicts established boundaries between sedentary and nomadic zones.
significance: Kanem-Bornu conflicts demonstrated the empire's military capacity against nomadic threats. The wars shaped Saharan political organization.

name: Mali-Songhai Wars
description: The conflicts between the Mali and Songhai empires for control of West African trade routes.
hook: Transition of West African hegemony from Mali to Songhai involved military conflict.
narrative: As Mali Empire declined in the 15th century, Songhai forces expanded militarily against Mali territories. Military victories enabled Songhai to seize control of former Mali dominions. The transition involved conquest of major Mali cities including Timbuktu.
significance: Mali-Songhai conflict redirected West African hegemony. Songhai dominance reorganized West African trade networks.

name: Songhai-Mali Conflicts
description: Conflicts between Songhai and Mali for West African dominance.
hook: Military conflicts during Mali's decline enabled Songhai rise to West African dominance.
narrative: Songhai's military expansion against Mali territories capitalized on Mali's declining power. Songhai forces conquered Mali core territories and trade centers. The conquest established Songhai as West African's dominant power.
significance: Songhai victory completed Mali's decline and initiated Songhai regional hegemony.

name: Vijayanagara Naval Wars
description: Vijayanagara's maritime conflicts and trade wars.
hook: The Vijayanagara Empire expanded maritime power and naval dominance in Indian Ocean waters.
narrative: Vijayanagara, primarily known as a land power, developed naval capabilities and conducted maritime campaigns. Naval wars involved control of Indian Ocean trade routes and coastal territories. The empire's naval expansion challenged regional maritime powers.
significance: Vijayanagara naval expansion established South Indian maritime interests. The campaigns influenced Indian Ocean trade patterns.

name: Yongle Emperor's Military Campaigns
description: Yongle's military campaigns consolidating Ming control of frontier regions.

name: Ming Invasion of Vietnam
description: Ming China invaded Vietnam, establishing Chinese occupation for 20 years before being expelled by Vietnamese resistance. This occupation temporarily brought Vietnam under Chinese rule.

name: Polish-Teutonic War (1409-1411)
description: The conflict between Poland and the Teutonic Knights that weakened the knights' power in the Baltic.

name: Decline of the Teutonic Order
description: The Teutonic Order was gradually defeated by Poland-Lithuania and Russia, losing their Baltic dominions. The Order's decline marked the end of crusading military orders in Europe.

name: Battle of Grunwald
description: The decisive Polish-Lithuanian victory over the Teutonic Knights that marked the beginning of their decline.
hook: 1410 battle where Polish-Lithuanian forces defeated the Teutonic Order and demonstrated eastern European military capability.
narrative: Polish forces under Wladyslaw II and Lithuanian forces under Vitovt decisively defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald. The battle involved massive cavalry charges and demonstrated superior Polish-Lithuanian military organization. The Order's military dominance was permanently broken.
significance: Grunwald established Polish-Lithuanian military superiority. The Order's decline presaged Prussian emergence as northern European power.

name: Battle of Agincourt
description: Henry V's decisive victory with a vastly outnumbered English force, reviving English fortunes in the war.

name: Ottoman-Venetian Wars
description: The wars between the Ottoman Empire and Venice over Eastern Mediterranean trade and territorial control.

name: Hussite Wars
description: The religious wars in Bohemia following Jan Hus's execution, mixing religious reform with military innovation.

name: Formation of Aztec Triple Alliance
description: Formation of the Triple Alliance with Mexico, Texcoco, and Tlacopan.

name: Aztec Wars Against the Tepanecs
description: Decisive Mexica rebellion against Tepanec overlords, led by Itzcoatl. Victory established the Aztec Triple Alliance and Mexica dominance in the Valley of Mexico for the next century.

name: Aztec War with Azcapotzalco
description: Aztec war against Azcapotzalco consolidating their power.

name: Aztec Flower Wars
description: Ritualized warfare by the Aztec Empire against neighboring city-states to capture warriors for sacrifice.

name: Battle of Orléans
description: Joan of Arc's victory that turned the tide of the war in France's favor, leading to ultimate French victory.

name: Siege of Angkor
description: Fall of Angkor to Siamese forces, ending Khmer hegemony.

name: Pachacuti's War Against the Chanca
description: Decisive Inca victory under Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui against the Chanca confederation. This battle transformed Pachacuti into a military genius and began the rapid Inca expansion that created an empire.

name: Inca Expansion
description: The rapid Inca expansion under Pachacuti that created the largest empire in pre-Columbian South America.
hook: Inca conquest extended empire from Ecuador to Chile under Pachacuti's successors (1471-1525).
narrative: Topa Inca (1471-1493) conquered northern Ecuador and southern Chile territories. Huayna Capac (1493-1525) extended empire to maximal extent but faced succession disputes following his death. Northern expansion incorporated new ethnic groups and facilitated administrative integration.
significance: Expansion achieved Inca hegemony over the entire Andean region. The expanded empire became the target of Spanish conquest.

name: Early Inca Expansion
description: Inca expansion campaigns consolidating Andean territories.
hook: Proto-Inca kingdom of Cusco expanded from a valley state to regional power through early military campaigns.
narrative: Before Pachacuti's dramatic expansion, Inca predecessors conducted military campaigns in the Cusco valley and surrounding regions. These early expansions established Inca military organization and tributary systems. Victories demonstrated Inca military capability and presaged later empire-building.
significance: Early Inca expansion established the administrative and military foundations for Pachacuti's imperial project. The campaigns created the political unity enabling rapid empire-building.

name: Albanian-Ottoman Wars (Skanderbeg)
description: Skanderbeg's resistance campaigns against Ottoman rule, becoming a legendary figure in Albanian history.

name: Tatar-Mongol Wars on Ming Border
description: Ming conflicts with nomadic tribes, including Tumu Crisis.

name: Tumu Crisis
description: Ming emperor captured, massive military defeat by Mongols.

name: Mutapa Internal Succession Wars
description: Internal succession disputes and civil conflicts within the Mutapa Empire.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Constantinople
description: Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople that ended the Byzantine Empire and established Ottoman dominance over the Eastern Mediterranean.
hook: Ottoman Mehmed's 1453 cannon bombardment of Constantinople ended the Byzantine Empire—the last vestige of Rome—and opened Europe to Ottoman expansion.
narrative: Constantinople, defended by 7,000 Byzantine soldiers and walls built 1,000 years prior, faced 80,000+ Ottoman besiegers with massive cannons (1453). The walls, unbreached for centuries, were bombarded by Ottoman artillery. After 53 days, Ottomans breached the walls; Emperor Constantine XI died defending the city. Last Christian bastion fell. Mehmed II established Ottoman dominance in the eastern Mediterranean and Balkans. Constantinople became Istanbul, center of Ottoman power for 400 years. Perhaps 50,000+ died in the siege and aftermath.
significance: Constantinople's fall symbolized Christianity's loss of the Eastern Mediterranean to Islamic rule. It prompted Western European anxiety about Ottoman expansion (lifting the Siege of Vienna 1683 became myth-making). The conquest redirected European exploration and trade toward Atlantic routes—Portuguese and Spanish exploration partly motivated by desire to bypass Ottoman-controlled trade. Ottoman dominance reshaped Mediterranean geopolitics for centuries. The conquest has become an icon in Turkish nationalism and Christian-Muslim historical narratives.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Ottoman Expansion in Aegean
description: Ottoman forces conquered the Aegean islands from Venetian and Genoese traders, extending Ottoman dominance throughout the Mediterranean. This conquest isolated Venice and gave Ottomans control of key maritime trade routes.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Greece
description: Ottoman forces gradually conquered Greek territories from the Byzantine successor states and Venetian colonies, establishing Ottoman control over the Balkans and Greece. This conquest lasted until Greek independence in the 19th century.

name: Siege of Constantinople (1453)
description: Fall of Constantinople ending Byzantine Empire and establishing Ottoman control.

name: Hundred Years' War - Individual Battles
description: Final English phase of conflicts ending with Tudor dynasty.

casualtyRange.notes: Major battles subset. Agincourt, Crecy, Poitiers and siege warfare.

name: Wars of the Roses
description: The English civil wars between the houses of York and Lancaster for control of the throne.

name: Aztec-Tlaxcalan Wars
description: Long-standing conflict between the Aztec Empire and the independent city-state of Tlaxcala.
hook: Aztec Empire and Tlaxcalan Confederacy conducted military campaigns and maintained tense tributary relationships.
narrative: Aztec emperors expanded into Tlaxcalan territories through military campaigns. Tlaxcalans resisted Aztec tributary demands while accepting selective trade and alliance. Conflicts involved siege warfare and raids. The relationship remained militarily tense despite periods of coexistence.
significance: Aztec-Tlaxcalan conflicts established the independence Tlaxcalans later leveraged in Spanish conquest. The Tlaxcalan military success presaged their later alliance with Cortés.

name: Wallachian-Ottoman Wars
description: The long conflict between Wallachia and the Ottomans, including Vlad III's resistance campaigns.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Serbia
description: Ottoman armies conquered Serbian kingdoms, incorporating the Balkans into the Ottoman Empire. Serbian resistance continued but was ultimately crushed by Ottoman military power.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Wallachia
description: Ottoman forces conquered Wallachia, establishing Ottoman hegemony in Eastern Europe despite the resistance of Vlad III. Wallachia became an Ottoman vassal state.

name: Vlad III's Campaign Against the Ottomans
description: Vlad III's famous resistance campaign against the Ottoman Empire using brutal tactics.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Bosnia
description: Ottoman forces conquered Bosnia from Hungarian control, establishing Ottoman dominance in the central Balkans. Bosnia became a core Ottoman province for centuries.

name: Turkish-Venetian Wars
description: Conflict between Ottoman and Venetian naval powers in Mediterranean.

name: Onin War
description: The ten-year war that devastated Kyoto and marked the beginning of Japan's Sengoku period.
hook: Decade-long 1467-1477 Kyoto conflict destroyed the Ashikaga shogunate and initiated Japanese feudal fragmentation.
narrative: The Onin War erupted from succession disputes within the Ashikaga shogunate, with two factions competing for the shogun's position. The conflict centered on Kyoto but devastated the capital and triggered the rise of independent daimyo. The war, ostensibly between the Yamana and Ōuchi clans, devolved into decades of feudal conflict. The Ashikaga shogunate's authority never recovered after Onin's conclusion. The period initiated the Sengoku ('Warring States') era of feudal fragmentation.
significance: The Onin War destroyed Japan's remaining centralized authority and initiated two centuries of feudal warfare. The destruction of Kyoto demonstrated military dominance's shift from court nobility to armed daimyo. The war's aftermath presaged the complete restructuring of Japanese political organization.

name: Sengoku Period (Japan)
description: The period of civil war in Japan between feudal daimyo that ended with unification under the Tokugawa.
hook: A century of Japanese warlord warfare created the conditions for national unification and samurai dominance.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) saw Japan fragment into competing domains (daimyo) fighting for supremacy. Major power centers included the Takeda, Uesugi, Imagawa, Oda, Toyotomi, and Tokugawa clans. Innovations included early firearms (introduced 1543), castle warfare, and conscripted peasant armies. Three towering figures emerged: Oda Nobunaga (1534-1582), who unified much of Japan; Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598), who completed unification; and Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616), who established a dynasty. Famous battles included Sekigahara (1600), where Tokugawa defeated the Toyotomi. The period's warfare was brutal, involving sieges and mass casualties.
significance: The Sengoku wars unified Japan politically and militarily. The Tokugawa Shogunate (1603-1868) provided unprecedented stability and isolation. The period elevated the samurai class and established bushido (the warrior code). The adoption of firearms transformed Japanese warfare. The period's unification created the conditions for Japan's rapid modernization in the 19th century.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Sengoku Period - Warring States Japan
description: Nearly 150 years of fragmented warfare between Japanese feudal lords (daimyo) saw the rise of powerful warlords who gradually unified Japan. The period ended with the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate and lasting peace.
hook: Japanese feudal lords (daimyo) waged unceasing warfare, creating a martial culture that unified the nation.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) saw Japan fragment into competing domains ruled by daimyo. The period began with the Onin War (1467-1477), which destroyed the Ashikaga shogunate's authority. Thereafter, daimyo fought constantly for territorial expansion and supremacy. Key military innovations included the adoption of firearms (introduced 1543) and changes in castle architecture to resist cannon fire. Three powerful daimyo eventually emerged: Oda Nobunaga (conquered much of central Japan), Toyotomi Hideyoshi (completed unification), and Tokugawa Ieyasu (established a stable shogunate). The period's warfare was characterized by large armies, complex logistics, and tactical innovation.
significance: The Sengoku wars unified Japan politically and militarily under the Tokugawa Shogunate, ushering in 250 years of stability. The period elevated the samurai class to dominance and established bushido (the warrior code). The period's military innovations influenced East Asian warfare. The unification created the conditions for Japan's rapid modernization in the 19th century and its emergence as a major Asian power.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sengoku Period - Warring States Japan
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Songhai Empire Expansion
description: Songhai Empire's expansion becoming the dominant West African power.
hook: Songhai Dynasty expanded territorial control across West Africa under successive emperors.
narrative: Songhai expansion under Ali and Askia incorporated vast West African territories. Military campaigns conquered rival powers and integrated them into tributary systems. Songhai military organization included professional cavalry and administrative structures.
significance: Songhai expansion created West Africa's largest pre-colonial state. The empire's administrative innovations influenced successor states.

name: Songhai Conquest of Timbuktu
description: Askia Muhammad's conquest of Timbuktu and consolidation of Songhai control over Mali.
hook: Songhai conquest of Timbuktu secured control of West Africa's major Islamic and commercial center.
narrative: Timbuktu, a major Islamic learning center and trade hub, fell to Songhai military conquest. The conquest gave Songhai control of critical intellectual and commercial resources. Songhai maintained Timbuktu's Islamic institutions.
significance: Timbuktu conquest consolidated Songhai dominance and demonstrated Songhai respect for Islamic learning.

name: Aztec-Tarascan Wars
description: Series of Aztec military campaigns to subdue the rival Tarascan Empire in Michoacán. The Aztecs were repulsed at Tzintzuntzan, establishing a disputed western border that neither power could decisively cross.

name: Inca Conquest of Chimú
description: Topa Inca's conquest of the Chimú Kingdom, adding the northern coast to Inca territory. This was the largest territorial acquisition of the later Inca expansion phase.
hook: Inca conquest of the Chimú Empire established Inca hegemony over Peruvian coastal regions.
narrative: The Chimú Empire, a major coastal power, controlled advanced irrigation systems and wealthy coastal territories. Inca forces, under Topa Inca or Pachacuti, conducted systematic conquest of Chimú territories. Chimú military resistance crumbled before Inca organization. The conquest integrated Chimú administrative expertise into Inca systems.
significance: Inca conquest of the Chimú established Inca dominance over coastal regions and integrated critical irrigation technology. The Chimú's administrative knowledge influenced Inca imperial organization.

name: Inca-Chimor Conquest
description: Inca conquest of Chimor, the largest pre-Inca civilization.
hook: Inca expansion incorporated the Chimor Empire and its coastal territories into the Inca realm.
narrative: The Inca conquest of Chimor (Chimú Empire) represented a major imperial expansion. Chimor's wealth and administrative sophistication made it a significant prize. Military campaigns reduced Chimor resistance. The conquest demonstrated Inca ability to assimilate complex coastal societies.
significance: Chimor conquest established Inca coastal control and integrated sophisticated Chimor administrative systems. The victory demonstrated Inca imperial capacity.

name: Diaguita Resistance to Inca Conquest
description: Ongoing Inca military campaigns to subdue the Diaguita peoples of northwestern Argentina and Chile. Diaguita resistance persisted throughout the Inca occupation until Spanish conquest.
hook: Diaguita people resisted Inca expansion in northwestern Argentina before Spanish colonization.
narrative: The Diaguita, living in northwestern Argentina, resisted Inca conquest through guerrilla warfare and fortified settlement defense. Despite Inca military superiority, Diaguita warriors maintained resistance across generations. Inca ultimately incorporated Diaguita territories but Diaguita culture persisted.
significance: Diaguita resistance demonstrated that Inca conquest was not inevitable and required sustained military effort. Diaguita cultural resilience influenced Andean colonial development.

name: Topa Inca's Expansion Wars
description: Extensive campaigns by Topa Inca to expand Inca territory south into modern Chile and Argentina, and east into the Amazon basin. Doubled the empire's territorial extent.
hook: Topa Inca's military campaigns expanded the Inca Empire into Ecuador and Chile (1471-1493).
narrative: Topa Inca succeeded Pachacuti and continued imperial expansion. His campaigns conquered northern Ecuador territories and extended Inca control southward into Chile. Northern expansion incorporated new ethnic groups and established Inca administrative control over vast new territories.
significance: Topa Inca's expansion achieved Inca hegemony over unprecedented Andean territories. The expanded empire created the imperial state confronting Spanish conquest.

name: Muscovite-Novgorod Wars
description: Muscovite conquest of Novgorod establishing Moscow dominance.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Moldavia
description: Ottoman forces conquered Moldavia, completing Ottoman conquest of the Balkans and establishing Ottoman control of the Danube region. Moldavia became an Ottoman vassal state like Wallachia.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Crimea
description: Ottoman forces conquered Crimea from Genoese and local rulers, establishing a Crimean Khanate as an Ottoman vassal. This conquest gave the Ottomans control of the Black Sea coast.

name: Sengoku Period Conflicts
description: Prolonged period of warfare between feudal lords (daimyo) with famous battles at Sekigahara and other sites.
hook: Japan's Sengoku warfare created a martial culture and military tradition that dominated East Asia for centuries.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) was characterized by constant warfare among daimyo (feudal lords) seeking territorial expansion. Armies grew from samurai-dominated forces to include conscripted peasants with firearms. Castles became increasingly sophisticated, driving innovations in fortification. Major campaigns included the Takeda-Uesugi rivalry (Kawanakajima battles), Oda Nobunaga's unification wars (defeating the Imagawa and Uesugi), and Toyotomi Hideyoshi's subjugation of remaining daimyo (siege of Odawara, 1590). The period's warfare was marked by rapid tactical evolution, from traditional samurai mounted combat to pike-and-shot infantry formations. By 1600, the Tokugawa Shogunate defeated the Toyotomi at Sekigahara, establishing a unified state.
significance: The Sengoku wars created a unified Japanese state under the Tokugawa Shogunate, enabling nearly 300 years of stability and prosperity. The period established Japanese military traditions (castle architecture, samurai codes) that persisted until modernization. The wars demonstrated the superiority of organized firearms over traditional samurai tactics. Japan's unification positioned it to resist European colonization and modernize rapidly in the 19th century.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Ottoman Conquest of Albania
description: Ottoman forces conquered Albania from Venice after a prolonged siege of Shkoder, establishing Ottoman control of the western Balkans. Albania remained Ottoman for over 400 years.

name: Decline of the Golden Horde
description: The fragmented remains of the Mongol Golden Horde were conquered or became vassals of the emerging Russian state and Ottoman Empire. This process marked the end of Mongol dominance in Eastern Europe.

name: Songhai Gao Expansion
description: Songhai expansion from Gao as a major West African imperial power.
hook: Songhai expansion extended hegemony over Gao and adjacent Niger River valley territories.
narrative: Gao, another major West African commercial center, fell to Songhai military campaigns. Gao's conquest completed Songhai control over critical Niger valley trade routes.
significance: Gao conquest solidified Songhai regional dominance and trade network control.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Herzegovina
description: Ottoman forces conquered Herzegovina, completing Ottoman control of the southern Balkans. Herzegovina became an Ottoman province for centuries.

name: Reconquista - Granada War
description: The final campaign of the Reconquista saw Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella conquer the last Muslim state in Iberia. This victory consolidated Spanish Christian power and freed resources for overseas expansion.

name: Conquest of Granada
description: The final campaign of the Reconquista that conquered the last Islamic emirate in Iberia.

name: Moldavian-Ottoman Wars
description: The prolonged conflicts between Moldavia and the Ottoman Empire for control of the region.

name: Battle of Bosworth Field
description: Henry VII's victory that ended the Wars of the Roses and established the Tudor dynasty.

name: Aztec Conquest of the Huasteca
description: Aztec conquest of the Huasteca region by Ahuitzotl, bringing the northern Gulf coast under Aztec tribute control.
hook: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire exploited internal divisions, indigenous allies, and epidemic disease.
narrative: Hernán Cortés arrived at Tenochtitlan in 1519 with 600 men, capturing Emperor Montezuma II as hostage. Montezuma's death and Cortés's retreat in the Night of Sorrows (June 1520) preceded Cortés's return with Tlaxcalan allies. Epidemic smallpox devastated the Aztec capital. The 93-day Siege of Tenochtitlan (May-August 1521) methodically starved the city. Cuauhtémoc's capture in August 1521 ended organized resistance.
significance: Aztec collapse within two years—facilitated by disease, indigenous alliances, and Spanish firepower—triggered Spanish America's foundation. The conquest introduced European infectious diseases killing millions.

name: Aztec Conquest of Soconusco
description: Aztec military campaign under Ahuitzotl to conquer the wealthy Soconusco region on the southern Pacific coast, bringing valuable tribute including cacao.
hook: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire exploited internal divisions, indigenous allies, and epidemic disease.
narrative: Hernán Cortés arrived at Tenochtitlan in 1519 with 600 men, capturing Emperor Montezuma II as hostage. Montezuma's death and Cortés's retreat in the Night of Sorrows (June 1520) preceded Cortés's return with Tlaxcalan allies. Epidemic smallpox devastated the Aztec capital. The 93-day Siege of Tenochtitlan (May-August 1521) methodically starved the city. Cuauhtémoc's capture in August 1521 ended organized resistance.
significance: Aztec collapse within two years—facilitated by disease, indigenous alliances, and Spanish firepower—triggered Spanish America's foundation. The conquest introduced European infectious diseases killing millions.

name: Ikko-Ikki Rebellions
description: Repeated rebellions by Buddhist-led peasant armies against feudal lords.

name: Ottoman-Venetian Trade Wars
description: A series of conflicts between Venice and the Ottoman Empire over trade routes and Mediterranean territories resulted in Venetian loss of dominance. Ottoman control of Mediterranean trade increased significantly.

name: Columbus Expeditions and Early Contact
description: Columbus's four voyages to the Caribbean and introduction of European conquest. Initiated the catastrophic Columbian Exchange affecting all subsequent American history.

name: Columbus Expeditions to the Americas
description: Christopher Columbus's expeditions initiated European contact with the Americas, leading to massive displacement and death of indigenous populations through conquest and disease. These voyages fundamentally reshaped world history and began Spanish colonial dominance in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Portuguese-Spanish Colonial Rivalry
description: Spain and Portugal divided the Americas through treaties and conflicts, with Spain dominating the majority. The division created the basis for modern Spanish and Portuguese-speaking Americas.
hook: Portugal and Spain competed to build global colonial empires, dividing the world between them.
narrative: Portuguese and Spanish colonial rivalry (15th-18th centuries) shaped the global colonial system. Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, pioneered ocean exploration and established trading posts along African coasts (1400s) and eventually reached India (Vasco da Gama, 1498). Spain, after supporting Columbus's expedition (1492), established colonies in the Americas. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the non-European world between Portugal and Spain. Portugal controlled territories in Africa, India, and Asia (Goa, Malacca, Brazil). Spain controlled most of the Americas. Competition erupted in the Pacific (the Philippines) and occasionally in military clashes (Battle of Diu, 1509). Both powers relied on superior naval technology and military superiority over indigenous peoples.
significance: Portuguese and Spanish colonial rivalry established the template for European colonialism and the global colonial system. The two nations' dominance in colonial ventures lasted until the 17th century, when the Dutch and English challenged their monopolies. The colonial competition resulted in the exploitation and decimation of indigenous populations, the transatlantic slave trade, and the transfer of vast wealth to Europe. The colonial empires shaped modern global inequalities and international relations. The legacy of Iberian colonialism persists in the cultural, linguistic, and religious identities of Latin America, Africa, and Asia.

name: Huayna Capac's Northern Campaigns
description: Inca expansion campaigns into Ecuador and the north. Huayna Capac extended Inca territory to modern Colombia while facing resistance.

name: First Italian War
description: French King Charles VIII invaded Italy, initiating a series of conflicts over Italian territory that would span six decades. This war established the pattern of European powers competing for control of the Italian peninsula.

name: Third Italian War
description: A series of conflicts over Italian territory concluded with Spanish dominance and the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, which established Spain as the major European power. These wars reshaped European political geography.

name: Italian Wars
description: The prolonged conflicts between Spain and France for control of Italy and its territories.
hook: European powers contended for control of Italy through military campaigns and dynastic diplomacy (1494-1559).
narrative: The Italian Wars pitted French kings against Spanish Habsburgs for dominance over Italian territories. The wars began with Charles VIII of France's invasion of Naples in 1494. Subsequent campaigns involved shifting alliances, papal involvement, and mercenary forces. Major battles included Marignano (1515, French victory), Pavia (1525, Spanish capture of Francis I), and the sack of Rome (1527, Spanish troops). The wars devastated Italian city-states and demonstrated the emerging power of centralized nation-states over Italian republican structures. The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559) established Spanish dominance over much of Italy.
significance: Italian Wars demonstrated the vulnerability of city-states to centralized national powers. The conflicts ended Italian independence and initiated Spanish-Habsburg dominance. The wars presaged the modern state system's emergence over medieval feudalism.

name: Fourth Ottoman-Venetian War
description: Ottoman-Venetian naval war in Mediterranean, resulting in Ottoman territorial gains.

name: Venetian-Ottoman War
description: The Ottoman Navy defeated Venice in several naval engagements, establishing Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean. Venice lost key territories including Greek possessions.

name: Second Italian War
description: France and Spain competed for control of Milan and Naples, with Spain ultimately establishing dominance in southern Italy. This war consolidated Spanish power in the Mediterranean.

name: American Indian Wars
description: Three centuries of conflict between European colonists and Native American peoples resulted in the near-total displacement of Native Americans. These wars transformed North American demographics and geography.
hook: Three centuries of indigenous resistance against European colonization fundamentally reshaped the Americas.
narrative: From the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519-1521) through the North American Indian Wars (1607-1890s), indigenous peoples fought colonizers across the continents. Initial Spanish conquests employed superior weaponry, disease, and alliances with indigenous rivals. North American conflicts saw tribes alternately ally with European powers (French, British) and adapt militarily—from mounted warfare on the Great Plains to ambush tactics in forests. Key moments included King Philip's War (1675), the Pueblo Revolt (1680), Tecumseh's Confederacy (1809), and the Great Sioux Wars (1876). The U.S. Army's systematic campaigns in the 1880s-1890s (Wounded Knee, Apache Wars) marked colonization's final phase.
significance: The wars resulted in the near-complete removal or displacement of indigenous peoples, the seizure of their lands, and the suppression of their sovereignty. Disease killed far more than warfare. The conflicts shaped the territorial expansion and ethnic composition of the United States and Canada. Contemporary indigenous rights movements trace their origins to this period of dispossession.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Aztec Tributary Uprisings
description: Periodic rebellions by tributary states against Aztec dominance. These revolts weakened empire cohesion and demonstrated resentment of Aztec rule.

name: Brazilian Indigenous Resistance to Portuguese
description: Centuries-long indigenous resistance to Portuguese colonial expansion. Tupi, Guaraní, and other groups resisted Portuguese settlement and enslavement.

name: Incan Provincial Revolts
description: Various provincial uprisings against Inca imperial rule in the decades before Spanish conquest. Demonstrated imperial vulnerability to internal revolt.
hook: Subject populations within the Inca Empire periodically rebelled against Inca tribute and rule.
narrative: Despite Inca administrative sophistication, subject peoples occasionally revolted against Inca control. Regional rebellions involved military campaigns to suppress resistance. Inca military response demonstrated imperial capacity to maintain dominance. Revolts provided opportunities for rival Inca factions to compete for imperial power.
significance: Provincial revolts demonstrated that Inca rule depended on military enforcement. The revolts created vulnerabilities exploitable during Spanish conquest.

name: Powhatan-Monacan Wars
description: Territorial conflicts between the powerful Powhatan Confederacy and the Monacan peoples of the Virginia Piedmont. Powhatan dominance was established by the time of European settlement.

name: Benin-Yoruba Conflicts
description: Territorial and commercial conflicts between Benin and neighboring Yoruba city-states.

name: Burmese-Mon Wars
description: Burmese forces gradually conquered and absorbed the Mon Kingdom, extending Burmese rule over lower Burma. This conquest created the modern extent of Burmese territory.
hook: Pyu, Mon, and Burman peoples competed for dominance over Burma through military conquest (6th-18th centuries).
narrative: The Pyu, an early Sino-Tibetan people, dominated central Burma until Burman migrations (9th-10th centuries) and the later Shan invasions. The Mon Kingdom controlled lower Burma from ancient times. Various Burman dynasties (Pagan, Ava, Toungoo, Konbaung) fought to control Mon territories and unify the region. Anawrahta of Pagan (1044-1077) unified much of Burma by conquering the Mon kingdom, establishing Pagan as a regional superpower. Subsequent dynasties continuously fought Mon resistance and Thai pressure. By the 18th century, the Konbaung Dynasty consolidated Burman control, but Mon cultural identity persisted.
significance: Burman-Mon conflicts established Burman political dominance despite Mon cultural significance. The unification process under successive dynasties created the Burmese state structure. Mon cultural traditions influenced Burmese art, religion, and governance.

name: Burmese-Siamese Wars
description: Centuries of warfare between Burma and Siam over control of mainland Southeast Asia resulted in significant territorial changes and population displacement. Both kingdoms remained major regional powers throughout this period.
hook: Centuries of conflicts between Burma and Siam determined control of Southeast Asian territory and regional dominance.
narrative: The Burmese-Siamese Wars (16th-19th centuries) were a series of conflicts between the Burmese and Siamese kingdoms for regional dominance. Major wars included the Burmese conquest of Siam under King Thaungyin (1550s-1560s), subsequent Siamese-Burmese conflicts (1600s), and the major war of 1824-1826. Burmese forces, particularly under King Alaungpaya (18th century), defeated Siam multiple times. The conflicts demonstrated the military superiority of Burmese cavalry and warfare tactics. The wars resulted in territorial changes, with Burma gaining influence over Siamese territories and populations. By the 19th century, both nations had become subordinated to British colonial rule (Burma directly; Siam maintained nominal independence).
significance: The Burmese-Siamese Wars demonstrated the power balance in Southeast Asia and established Burma as a major regional power until British colonization. The wars' outcome influenced territorial boundaries and the ethnic composition of modern Burma and Thailand. The conflicts influenced Southeast Asian politics and the historical narratives of both nations. The wars' legacy contributed to modern Thai-Myanmar tensions and territorial disputes. The conflicts demonstrated the military effectiveness of Southeast Asian kingdoms before European colonization.

name: Cambodian-Thai Wars
description: Conflicts between Cambodia and Siam resulted in Thai expansion and Cambodian contraction, reducing Cambodia to a vassal state. These wars reshaped Southeast Asian power dynamics.

name: French-Spanish Colonial Wars
description: Centuries of conflict between France and Spain over colonial territories in North America and the Caribbean resulted in gradual French expansion. The conflicts concluded with British dominance in North America.

name: Hausa-Fulani Conflicts
description: Territorial and cultural conflicts between Hausa city-states and Fulani pastoralists.

name: Ottoman-Circassian Wars
description: Ottoman conflicts with Caucasian peoples including Circassians resulted in massive depopulation and displacement. Ottoman control of the Caucasus remained contested against local resistance.

name: Ottoman-Georgian Wars
description: Georgian kingdoms faced pressure from both Ottoman and Persian powers, gradually coming under Ottoman and Russian influence. Georgia became a contested borderland between empires.

name: Ottoman-Hungarian Wars
description: A century of warfare between the Ottomans and Hungary resulted in Ottoman conquest of much of Hungary. These conflicts lasted until the Treaty of Zsitvatorok in 1606.

casualtyRange.notes: 1500-1606. Multiple conflicts and sieges. Ottoman expansion into Hungary.

hook: Ottoman expansion collided with Hungarian resistance, reshaping the balance of power in Southeast Europe.
narrative: The Ottoman Empire's expansion into Southeast Europe (15th-16th centuries) brought it into conflict with Hungary, a major Christian kingdom. The Ottoman-Hungarian Wars included multiple campaigns and devastating Ottoman victories. The Battle of Mohács (1526) was a catastrophic Hungarian defeat that left the kingdom divided and Ottoman-dominated. Ottoman forces advanced toward Vienna but were halted at the Gates of Vienna (1529). Successive Ottoman-Hungarian conflicts (16th-17th centuries) saw the Ottomans gradually advance westward. The Ottoman conquest of Hungary demonstrated superior military organization, logistics, and the effectiveness of Ottoman janissaries (elite infantry) and cavalry.
significance: The Ottoman-Hungarian Wars established Ottoman dominance in Southeast Europe and blocked further westward expansion. The wars prevented Ottoman conquest of Central Europe (though Vienna was threatened). The conflicts demonstrated the resilience of Christian kingdoms against Ottoman advance. The wars' outcome reshaped the balance of power between the Ottoman and European worlds. The conflicts influenced European perceptions of the Ottoman threat and motivated Christian unity efforts.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Polish-Ottoman Conflicts
description: Centuries of conflicts between Poland-Lithuania and the Ottoman Empire over territorial control of Eastern Europe and the Balkans resulted in Ottoman expansion to Europe. Poland ultimately declined as Ottoman power waned.

name: Portuguese Expansion in Africa
description: Portuguese explorers and traders established coastal fortresses and trading posts across Africa, beginning European colonization of the continent. Portuguese naval superiority allowed them to dominate African coastal trade for two centuries.

name: Portuguese Conquest of Brazil
description: Portuguese conquistadors and settlers gradually conquered Brazil from indigenous peoples and competing European powers, establishing Portugal's largest and most valuable colony. The conquest devastated indigenous populations through warfare and disease.
hook: Portugal colonized Brazil through gradual settlement, indigenous enslavement, and transplantation of African slaves.
narrative: After Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500, Portugal slowly established trading posts and colonies along Brazil's coast. Initial indigenous resistance (Tupí, Guató, and other groups) impeded early settlement. By the 1530s, the crown granted hereditary captaincies to encourage colonization. Portuguese settlers enslaved indigenous peoples for labor; when disease and flight depleted this workforce, they turned to the transatlantic slave trade (beginning 1538). Competition with the French spurred Portuguese expansion inland. Key developments included the founding of Rio de Janeiro (1565) and São Paulo (1554), and conflicts with rival European powers for colonial dominance. By 1750, Portugal controlled much of the continent.
significance: Brazil became the world's largest slave society, importing 4.9 million enslaved Africans—more than any other destination. This created a mixed-race, plantation-based colonial society fundamentally different from Spanish America. Brazil's racial demographics and social structure were forged through this conquest and enslavement. The conflict established Portugal as a major Atlantic power.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Russian-Polish Conflicts
description: Centuries of conflicts between Russia and Poland-Lithuania over Eastern Europe resulted in Polish decline and Russian expansion. Russia ultimately partitioned Poland by 1795.
hook: Centuries of warfare between Russia and Poland determined control of Eastern Europe and shaped regional geopolitics.
narrative: Russian-Polish conflicts (14th-18th centuries) were recurrent struggles for dominance in Eastern Europe. Early conflicts included the Teutonic Order, Polish, and Russian competition in the region. Major wars included Poland-Lithuania's rise to power (16th-17th centuries) and subsequent Russian expansion. The Russo-Polish War (1654-1667) saw Russia conquer significant Polish-Lithuanian territories. Peter the Great's wars against Sweden (Great Northern War) also involved Polish territories. By the late 18th century, Russia had become the dominant power, and through the Partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795), Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided Poland among themselves. The conflicts drove Polish partition and subjugation until Polish independence (1918).
significance: Russian-Polish conflicts established Russia as the dominant Eastern European power and facilitated the partitions of Poland. The conflicts' outcome left Poland divided and subjugated until the 20th century. The wars influenced Polish national identity and resistance to Russian rule. Polish-Russian tensions persisted into the modern era, shaping Cold War politics and contemporary European tensions. The conflicts demonstrated the vulnerability of intermediate powers to pressure from stronger neighbors.

name: Spanish Expansion in North Africa
description: Spanish forces conquered several North African coastal enclaves and fought Ottoman and Moroccan forces for regional dominance. Spanish control remained limited to small coastal areas.

name: Vietnamese Expansion South - Nam Vu
description: Vietnamese states gradually conquered the Kingdom of Champa and expanded southward into the Mekong Delta, creating modern Vietnam's territorial extent. This expansion displaced numerous Southeast Asian populations and established Vietnamese dominance in Indochina.

name: Safavid Empire Formation
description: The Safavid Dynasty conquered Persia, establishing Shia Islam as the state religion and creating a major Islamic empire. The Safavids rivaled the Ottomans for centuries as the dominant Middle Eastern power.
hook: Shiite militant movement conquered Persia, establishing the Safavid Empire as Islam's major Shiite power.
narrative: The Safavid movement, founded by Safi al-Din Ardabili, began as a Sufi mystical order but transformed into a militant political force. Under Ismail I (r. 1501-1524), the Safavids conquered Persia (modern-day Iran) through a series of military campaigns. Ismail's forces, fired by religious zeal, defeated rival dynasties (Aq Qoyunlu, various local lords) and established Shiite Islam as the state religion. The conquest of Persia created a major Shiite power rivaling the Sunni Ottoman Empire.
